p01.why: <=> does not accept two array operands.

p02.why: Integer <=> gives strong_ordering with less, equal, and greater as the values order.

p03.why: The order of elements and members carries into their subobjects, so both comparisons are true.

p04.why: Floating-point <=> gives partial_ordering, 1.0 is less than 2.0, and a NaN operand gives unordered.

p05.why: Comparing two arrays is valid but Clang and GCC warn under -Wall -Wextra, and -Werror makes the warning an error.

p06.why: <=> does not compare a function pointer with nullptr.

p07.why: <=> between a pointer and literal 0 is not valid; Clang and GCC reject it, and EDG accepts it.

p08.why: Both operands are arrays, even though they are the same array.

p09.why: On x86-64 long holds every unsigned value, so the common type is long and nothing narrows.

p10.why: The explicit cast silences the sign-compare warning, so -Werror has nothing to promote.

p11.why: Pointers are equal when they hold the same address or are both null, and nullptr equals literal 0.

p12.why: Equality of addresses of two distinct static objects, and with nullptr, is a constant and gives the expected results.

p13.why: A member that occupies no storage has an unspecified order, and the Evidence says all three implementations give a result during constant evaluation.

p14.why: Pointers into members of two elements of one array follow the element order, and constant evaluation can compare them.

p15.why: Pointers that differ in cv-qualifiers at any level compare for equality through a type with const added where needed.

p16.why: D* converts to B*, and the converted pointer equals p.

p17.why: Relational comparison of pointers to unrelated objects is not a constant expression.

p18.why: Two values of the same scoped enumeration can be compared.

p19.why: The int operand converts to unsigned, -Wsign-compare warns, and -Werror makes it an error.

p20.why: Rows have no gap, so the end of one row equals the start of the next, and pointers into two rows are ordered during constant evaluation.

p21.why: -1 does not fit in unsigned, so converting it narrows, and <=> rejects narrowing.

p22.why: A relational comparison of a pointer with literal 0 is not valid; Clang and GCC reject, and EDG accepts.

p23.why: With -m32 long and unsigned have the same size, the common type is unsigned long, and converting a long narrows.

p24.why: int* and double* are pointers to unrelated types.

p25.why: Pointers into one array compare in index order, with the one-past pointer last.

p26.why: The built-in <=> copies the static member that names the result, so the custom values -7, 5, and 9 come through.

p27.why: A pointer cannot be compared with an integer other than literal 0.

p28.why: Every comparison with a NaN is false except !=, so no early return fires.

p29.why: Arithmetic and unscoped enumeration operands convert to a common type and each assertion is true; A > 2.5 draws only a deprecation warning.

p30.why: Comparing two arrays draws a warning under -Wall -Wextra, and -Werror makes it an error.

p31.why: Without -Werror the array comparison is valid; each array becomes a pointer to its first element.

p32.why: <=> does not compare two values of the type of nullptr.

p33.why: int* converts to void*, so equality is valid.

p34.why: The order is unspecified, but lt || gt || !lt is always true.

p35.why: A scoped enumeration cannot be compared with an integer.

p36.why: Clang and GCC give true for an object and its first member as void*, and EDG gives false, so EDG fails the static_assert.

p37.why: The result is unspecified, but at run time two distinct objects have different addresses, so exactly one of < and > is true; the specification does not promise this.

p38.why: Union member pointers have an unspecified order, and all three implementations give a result during constant evaluation.

p39.why: -1 converts to the largest unsigned value, and on x86-64 -1L < 0u compares in long and is true.

p40.why: Two members of a union hold the same address, so the pointers are equal.

p41.why: A relational comparison of two function pointers is valid with an unspecified result; there is no main.

p42.why: A chained comparison; GCC and Clang 22 diagnose it under -Wparentheses and -Werror rejects, and Clang 18 gives no warning for variables and accepts.

p44.why: The A subobject through B and through C are two different subobjects, so p1 != p2, and p1 == p3.

p45.why: Whether a + 1 equals b is unspecified, but r || !r is always true.

p46.why: int* converts to const int*, so both comparisons are valid.

p47.why: Relational and equality operators give bool.

p48.why: Union member order is unspecified, the result is discarded, and main returns 0.

p49.why: All comparisons with a NaN are false except !=.

p50.why: int and object pointers give strong_ordering, and double gives partial_ordering.

p51.why: An unscoped enumeration and an integer are valid <=> operands.

p52.why: Only one operand is an array, so it becomes a pointer, and a[0] comes before a[1].

p53.why: Relational binds tighter than equality and each group associates left, so each assertion holds; an equality chain is not a chained comparison in CMP-14.

p54.why: left < middle > right is chained; GCC and Clang 22 diagnose it and -Werror rejects, while Clang 18 does not warn for variables.

p55.why: -0.0 and 0.0 are equal, so both give equivalent.

p56.why: Comparing an unscoped enumeration with a double is deprecated and the compilers warn; I assume the warning is on by default, which the specification does not say, and -Werror makes it an error.

p57.why: Members compare in declaration order, so &s.a < &s.b.

p58.why: Member pointers that select the same member of the same subobject are equal, and null member pointers compare equal to nullptr only.

p59.why: short and signed char promote to int, so -1 < 1 holds, while int against unsigned types converts -1 to the largest value.

p60.why: Parentheses around the inner comparison silence the chained-comparison warning.

p61.why: Values of two different scoped enumerations cannot be compared.

p62.why: Pointers into an array member and the member after it follow declaration order, and every compiler accepts these during constant evaluation.

p63.why: Comparing one past a with b is rejected during constant evaluation by Clang and GCC, and accepted by EDG.

p64.why: Values of one scoped enumeration compare by their values.

p65.why: Clang 22 rejects a chained comparison by default; Clang 18, GCC, and EDG accept, and (3 > 2) > 1 is false, so the assertion holds.

p66.why: <=> does not compare pointers to members.

p67.why: A function pointer and void* cannot be compared.

p68.why: The end of row 2 equals the start of row 3, so end == next and end < next is false.

p69.why: A noexcept function pointer compares with a plain function pointer of the same type.

p70.why: Relational comparison of two nullptr_t values is not valid; Clang and GCC reject, and EDG accepts.

p71.why: <=> between an unscoped enumeration and a floating-point value is rejected by Clang and GCC and accepted by EDG.

p72.why: An object and its first member share an address on Clang and GCC, and the second member has a different address.

p73.why: Comparing two different enumerations is deprecated, -Wdeprecated warns, and -Werror makes it an error.

p74.why: A relational comparison of a pointer with nullptr is not valid; Clang and GCC reject, and EDG accepts.

p75.why: Array comparison compares addresses, which Clang and GCC accept in strict mode and in constant evaluation; the deprecation warning does not stop translation.

p76.why: <=> on pointers to unrelated objects is not a constant expression.

p77.why: Pointers to members cannot be compared with a relational operator.

p78.why: Each constant fits the converted type, unsigned char and int both become int, and int with long long or float with double do not narrow.

p79.why: <=> does not compare two different unscoped enumerations.

p80.why: <=> binds tighter than ==, so the expression is (1 <=> 2) == less.

p81.why: Integer to floating-point is not counted as narrowing for <=>, and the result is partial_ordering.

p82.why: std::strong_ordering is not declared before <=> is used.

p83.why: Two nullptr values are equal, two null member pointers are equal, and a non-null member pointer differs from null.

p84.why: <=> does not compare two function pointers.

p85.why: The results are unspecified but the comparisons are valid, and main returns 0.

p86.why: a < b < c is chained; GCC and Clang 22 diagnose it and -Werror rejects, while Clang 18 does not warn for variables.

p87.why: <=> does not accept a bool with an operand of another type.
